topic: The Teacher and the School Curriculum
subtopic: Curriculum Foundations, Design Models, Implementation, & DepEd Matatag/K-12

items.definition: Derived from the Latin word 'currere' meaning 'to run a course' or racecourse; encompasses the total planned learning experiences, contents, and outcomes designed for learners under school guidance.
items.rationalization: In modern education, curriculum is not merely a syllabus or textbook list, but all guided learning experiences provided to students.

mnemonic.title: Curriculum Root
mnemonic.phrase: Currere Means Running the Academic Course

items.tosCompetency: Define curriculum concepts, nature, and scope

items.definition: The curriculum proposed and endorsed by professional organizations, policy-making bodies, or government agencies like DepEd, CHED, TESDA, and UNESCO.
items.rationalization: CHED CMOs and DepEd Curriculum Guides are prime examples of recommended curricula that set national standards.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The formalized curriculum documents produced by curriculum writers and educators, including lesson plans, syllabi, course modules, textbooks, and curriculum guides.
items.rationalization: When a teacher prepares a Daily Lesson Log (DLL) or Detailed Lesson Plan (DLP), they are operationalizing the written curriculum.

mnemonic.title: Written Curriculum
mnemonic.phrase: Black on White Documents for Teaching

items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The actual instructional activities, methodologies, demonstrations, and learning experiences implemented by the teacher inside the classroom.
items.rationalization: What the teacher actually delivers and how students engage with content constitutes the taught curriculum; varies by teacher style.

mnemonic.title: Taught Curriculum
mnemonic.phrase: Taught is What Truly Transpires in Class

items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The physical resources, instructional materials, laboratories, library books, multimedia devices, and learning facilities that assist in curriculum delivery.
items.rationalization: Without adequate science labs, computers, and reading materials, the supported curriculum is deficient, hindering taught curriculum effectiveness.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The tested, evaluated, and measured curriculum through paper-and-pencil tests, performance tasks, portfolios, and national examinations like the NAT.
items.rationalization: Assessed curriculum measures the extent of student achievement against learning competencies through formative and summative instruments.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The actual learning outcomes, knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes that students retain, demonstrate, and apply in real life as a result of schooling.
items.rationalization: The bottom line of all educational efforts; if students do not change behavior or gain competence, the curriculum was not truly learned.

mnemonic.title: Learned Curriculum
mnemonic.phrase: Learned is the Lasting Legacy in Learners

items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The unintended, unwritten, informal curriculum consisting of school climate, teacher attitudes, peer peer dynamics, social norms, and unspoken rules absorbed by students.
items.rationalization: Students learn punctuality, obedience, gender roles, or competitiveness implicitly from classroom routines even if not stated in objectives.

mnemonic.title: Hidden Curriculum
mnemonic.phrase: Unspoken Lessons Learnt in the Shadows

items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The topics, perspectives, concepts, and issues that are consciously or unconsciously excluded and not taught in school (what schools do not teach).
items.rationalization: Formulated by Elliot Eisner; omitting sensitive topics like sex education, indigenous perspectives, or specific historical conflicts constitutes the null curriculum.

mnemonic.title: Null Curriculum
mnemonic.phrase: Null is Nothing Taught or Not Included

items.tosCompetency: Distinguish types of curricula operating in schools

items.definition: The classical linear-deductive curriculum development model based on four fundamental questions: Purpose, Learning experiences, Organization, and Evaluation.
items.rationalization: Tyler posits that curriculum development begins with formulating clear behavioral objectives, selecting and organizing learning experiences, and evaluating outcomes.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze curriculum development models and theories

items.definition: An inductive, teacher-led curriculum development model arguing that teachers who teach the curriculum should be the primary designers, starting from specifics to generalizations.
items.rationalization: Taba identified 7 steps: Diagnosis of needs, Formulation of objectives, Selection of content, Organization of content, Selection of learning experiences, Organization of learning experiences, and Determination of what to evaluate.

mnemonic.title: Taba's Model
mnemonic.phrase: Teachers at the Grassroots Create Curriculum

items.tosCompetency: Analyze curriculum development models and theories

items.definition: A curriculum design organized strictly around separate academic disciplines (e.g., Math, Science, History, English) focusing on content mastery and textbook sequence.
items.rationalization: The oldest and most common design; criticized for fragmenting knowledge and neglecting student interests, but praised for easy organization and logical structure.
items.tosCompetency: Differentiate curriculum design models

items.definition: A curriculum design built around the needs, interests, developmental abilities, and experiences of the individual learner, inspired by John Dewey's progressivism.
items.rationalization: Includes child-centered design, experience-centered design, and humanistic design where learners actively participate in choosing and pursuing projects.

mnemonic.title: Learner-Centered
mnemonic.phrase: Child at the Center of Classroom

items.tosCompetency: Differentiate curriculum design models

items.definition: A curriculum design organized around real-world societal problems, persistent life situations, community issues, and human survival challenges.
items.rationalization: Draws from social reconstructionism; trains learners to analyze societal dilemmas like climate change, poverty, corruption, and design actionable solutions.
items.tosCompetency: Differentiate curriculum design models

items.definition: An instructional approach where key concepts are introduced early in simple forms and revisited repeatedly at increasing levels of depth and complexity across grade levels.
items.rationalization: The foundational organizing principle of the Philippine K to 12 basic education curriculum, enabling mastery without abrupt conceptual leaps.

mnemonic.title: Spiral Progression
mnemonic.phrase: Bruner Loops Back Deeper and Wider

items.tosCompetency: Explain spiral progression and curriculum organizing principles

items.definition: The breadth and depth of content, topics, learning competencies, and experiences covered within a curriculum at any given grade level.
items.rationalization: Scope defines 'how much' and 'what' is covered, establishing the boundaries of the curriculum syllabus.

mnemonic.title: Curriculum Scope
mnemonic.phrase: Scope is the Sea of Subject Matter

items.tosCompetency: Identify curriculum organization criteria and dimensions

items.definition: The order, progression, and chronological or logical arrangement of learning topics and competencies over time.
items.rationalization: Can be sequenced from simple to complex, prerequisite to dependent, concrete to abstract, or chronological (historical).
items.tosCompetency: Identify curriculum organization criteria and dimensions

items.definition: The vertical recurrence and repeated exposure to pervasive curriculum concepts, skills, and values over time to build enduring competence.
items.rationalization: Continuity ensures that essential skills like reading comprehension or scientific inquiry are practiced consistently from elementary through senior high.
items.tosCompetency: Identify curriculum organization criteria and dimensions

items.definition: The horizontal linking and cross-disciplinary blending of concepts across different subject areas, demonstrating how knowledge is interconnected.
items.rationalization: For example, connecting a Science lesson on deforestation with an Economics lesson on resource allocation and an English essay assignment.
items.tosCompetency: Identify curriculum organization criteria and dimensions

items.definition: The smooth vertical and horizontal alignment of curriculum elements, ensuring that grade-to-grade transitions (vertical) and subject connections (horizontal) are seamless without gaps or redundancies.
items.rationalization: Vertical articulation prevents grade 7 teachers from assuming students learned skills that Grade 6 never taught; horizontal articulation aligns parallel subjects.
items.tosCompetency: Identify curriculum organization criteria and dimensions

items.definition: The equitable distribution of time, weight, emphasis, and resources among cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains, as well as subject disciplines.
items.rationalization: Prevents over-emphasizing rote memorization at the expense of creative arts, physical health, or moral values development.

mnemonic.title: Curriculum Balance
mnemonic.phrase: Equal Weights on the Educational Scale

items.tosCompetency: Identify curriculum organization criteria and dimensions

items.definition: The degree of congruence and consistency among curriculum standards, instructional activities, learning objectives, and assessment methods (Constructive Alignment).
items.rationalization: John Biggs' constructive alignment states that what is stated in the objective must match what is taught in activities and measured in tests.
items.tosCompetency: Apply constructive alignment principles to lesson planning

items.definition: The systematic process of indexing and diagramming curriculum content, competencies, standards, and assessments over an academic calendar to identify redundancies and misalignments.
items.rationalization: Creates curriculum maps that allow teachers and administrators to visually audit what is actually taught across grades.
items.tosCompetency: Examine curriculum mapping techniques and tools

items.definition: The phase of the curriculum development cycle where the written curriculum is put into actual operational practice in schools and classrooms by teachers and administrators.
items.rationalization: Ornstein and Hunkins define implementation as a process of educational change requiring teacher professional development, resource provision, and leadership support.

mnemonic.title: Curriculum Implementation
mnemonic.phrase: Putting Plans into Practical Classroom Practice

items.tosCompetency: Describe the curriculum implementation process

items.definition: The formal determination of the quality, effectiveness, relevance, and value of a curriculum program to make decisions about its continuation, modification, or termination.
items.rationalization: Uses formative evaluation during implementation to improve materials and summative evaluation at the end to judge overall program impact.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze curriculum evaluation methods and purposes

items.definition: A comprehensive decision-oriented curriculum evaluation framework analyzing four components: Context (needs/goals), Input (resources/strategies), Process (implementation), and Product (outcomes).
items.rationalization: CIPP helps educational administrators evaluate whether a reform met community needs, had adequate resources, was executed properly, and produced desired student gains.
items.tosCompetency: Apply curriculum evaluation models (CIPP, Tyler)

items.definition: The multi-faceted professional role of a teacher as a Knower, Writer, Planner, Initiator, Innovator, Implementer, and Evaluator of curriculum.
items.rationalization: Teachers are not passive transmitters of curriculum guides; they interpret, adapt, enrich, and innovate curriculum materials for their specific classroom context.

mnemonic.title: 7 Roles of Curricularist
mnemonic.phrase: Knows, Writes, Plans, Initiates, Innovates, Implements, Evaluates

items.tosCompetency: Characterize the teacher's roles as a curricularist

items.definition: Individuals and groups who have an active interest, influence, or investment in the curriculum, including learners, teachers, school managers, parents, community leaders, and industry partners.
items.rationalization: Learners are the core stakeholders; teachers are implementers; parents are partners and co-financiers; community provides authentic contexts.
items.tosCompetency: Identify roles of stakeholders in curriculum development

items.term: Republic Act No. 10533 (Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013)
items.definition: The statutory law establishing the K to 12 Basic Education Program in the Philippines, adding Kindergarten and two years of Senior High School (Grades 11-12).
items.rationalization: Aimed to make Filipino graduates globally competitive, ready for employment, entrepreneurship, middle-level skills, or higher education.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze legal bases of Philippine curriculum reforms

items.definition: The curriculum policy under RA 10533 prescribing the use of the learner's native mother tongue as the medium of instruction and subject from Kindergarten to Grade 3.
items.rationalization: Research proves children learn to read and comprehend faster when instructed first in their mother tongue before bridging to Filipino and English.
items.tosCompetency: Explain language policies and MTB-MLE in Philippine curriculum

items.definition: The specialized curriculum pathways under K to 12: Academic Track (STEM, ABM, HUMSS, GAS), TVL (Technical-Vocational-Livelihood), Sports Track, and Arts & Design Track.
items.rationalization: Provides contextualized career preparation aligned with students' aptitude, interest, and post-secondary aspirations.
items.tosCompetency: Identify SHS tracks and strands under RA 10533

items.definition: The revised basic education curriculum launched by DepEd to decongest learning competencies by 70%, focusing on foundational literacy, numeracy, and socio-emotional skills.
items.rationalization: MATATAG stands for: MA-Making curriculum relevant; TA-Taking steps to accelerate services; TA-Taking good care of learners; G-Giving support to teachers.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze recent DepEd curriculum innovations (MATATAG)

items.definition: Benchmark statements in the DepEd curriculum that describe what students should know, understand, and be able to grasp conceptually at each grade level.
items.rationalization: Answers the question: 'What do students need to know?' Formulates the baseline conceptual knowledge required of learners.
items.tosCompetency: Differentiate Content Standards, Performance Standards, and MELCs

items.definition: Benchmark statements that specify what students should be able to do, perform, produce, or demonstrate with the knowledge and understanding they have acquired.
items.rationalization: Answers the question: 'What can students do with what they know?' Evaluated via authentic performance tasks and rubrics.
items.tosCompetency: Differentiate Content Standards, Performance Standards, and MELCs

items.definition: The prioritized set of competencies identified by DepEd that learners must acquire to transition successfully to the next grade level or life stage, even during crises.
items.rationalization: Created during the COVID-19 pandemic to streamline the curriculum into enduring, indispensable skills rather than nice-to-know details.
items.tosCompetency: Differentiate Content Standards, Performance Standards, and MELCs

items.definition: A curriculum design framework by Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe that plans backwards in 3 stages: 1. Identify Desired Results; 2. Determine Acceptable Evidence; 3. Plan Learning Experiences.
items.rationalization: Reverses traditional planning (which starts with activities or textbooks); begins with the desired transfer of big ideas and essential questions.

mnemonic.title: UbD Backward Design
mnemonic.phrase: Results First, Evidence Second, Plan Third

items.tosCompetency: Apply Understanding by Design (UbD) framework

items.definition: Open-ended, thought-provoking questions that recur throughout inquiry, spark genuine wonder, and point to the core big ideas of a discipline.
items.rationalization: Not simple factual queries with single right answers; e.g., 'What is justice?' or 'How do organisms adapt to survive?'
items.tosCompetency: Apply Understanding by Design (UbD) framework

items.definition: The educational process of relating the curriculum content and competencies to the local setting, culture, daily life, and environment of the learners.
items.rationalization: Mandated by RA 10533 to make learning relevant; includes localization and indigenization.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish localization from indigenization in curriculum

items.definition: Adapting curriculum delivery and instructional materials by using local information, materials, and examples from the learners' immediate community without altering standards.
items.rationalization: For example, using coconut shells or bamboo instead of commercial test tubes, or using local barangay crop data for Math statistics.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish localization from indigenization in curriculum

items.definition: A deeper level of contextualization that embeds the indigenous knowledge systems, practices, worldviews, values, and languages of an IP community into the curriculum design.
items.rationalization: Requires consulting indigenous elders and community members to ensure cultural integrity and respectful curricular integration (IPEd framework).
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish localization from indigenization in curriculum

items.definition: Modifying curriculum content, instructional process, products, or learning environment based on student readiness levels, interests, and learning profiles.
items.rationalization: Associated with Carol Ann Tomlinson; provides varied pathways so all learners achieve mastery regardless of starting point.
items.tosCompetency: Design differentiated curricular tasks for diverse learners

items.definition: A Table of Specifications (TOS) that blueprints the distribution of test items across Bloom's cognitive taxonomy levels and curriculum learning competencies.
items.rationalization: Ensures test items have content validity and accurately reflect the time and cognitive depth spent during instruction.
items.tosCompetency: Construct and evaluate a Table of Specifications (TOS)

items.definition: A minor curriculum alteration where one textbook, resource, or instructional unit is replaced by another without altering the fundamental curriculum structure.
items.rationalization: E.g., replacing an outdated Grade 8 Science textbook with a newly approved edition.
items.tosCompetency: Categorize types of curriculum change

items.definition: Modifying existing curriculum materials, content, or time allocations to introduce new items without overhauling basic goals.
items.rationalization: E.g., adding an internet safety module into an existing Computer subject or adjusting the class time from 60 to 45 minutes.

mnemonic.title: Alteration Change
mnemonic.phrase: Adjusting and Adding to Existing Content

items.tosCompetency: Categorize types of curriculum change

items.definition: A major, systemic reform that reorganizes the entire structure, sequence, philosophy, and grade level composition of the educational system.
items.rationalization: The shift from the 10-year Basic Education Curriculum (RBEC) to the K to 12 Enhanced Basic Education Program (RA 10533) is a prime example of restructuring.

mnemonic.title: Restructuring Change
mnemonic.phrase: Radical Reorganization of the Whole System

items.tosCompetency: Categorize types of curriculum change

items.definition: Disruptive changes that disturb existing schedules or routines, often initiated from external pressures, requiring temporary or permanent adjustments.
items.rationalization: E.g., sudden shift to blended learning during pandemic typhoons or extreme heat advisories adjusting class hours.
items.tosCompetency: Categorize types of curriculum change

items.definition: The psychological and behavioral hesitation of teachers toward curricular reforms, typically caused by lack of training, insufficient materials, time constraints, or habit.
items.rationalization: Successful curriculum implementers overcome resistance through clear communication, collaborative leadership, supportive coaching, and resource provision.

mnemonic.title: Curriculum Resistance
mnemonic.phrase: Change Calls for Coaching and Comfort

items.tosCompetency: Analyze factors affecting curriculum implementation and resistance

items.definition: A curriculum design approach (championed by William Spady) that starts with a clear specification of what students should be able to demonstrate upon graduation, organizing curriculum backwards to achieve those outcomes.
items.rationalization: Adopted in Philippine Higher Education via CHED CMO 46 s. 2012, emphasizing Program Educational Objectives (PEOs) and Student Outcomes (SOs).

mnemonic.title: Outcomes-Based Education
items: B - Backward design from exit outcomes

items.tosCompetency: Explain Outcomes-Based Education (OBE) in tertiary curriculum

items.definition: The national reference system that describes educational qualification levels (Levels 1 to 8) based on learning outcomes, aligning Philippine credentials with ASEAN and international standards.
items.rationalization: Baccalaureate degrees (including BSEd/BEEd) are designated as PQF Level 6; Master's is Level 7; Doctoral is Level 8.

mnemonic.title: PQF Levels
mnemonic.phrase: Level 6 for Bachelors, 7 for Masters, 8 for Doctors

items.tosCompetency: Analyze PQF levels and qualification descriptors

items.definition: The dichotomy between strictly implementing curriculum materials exactly as written by curriculum designers (fidelity) versus tailoring and modifying them to suit classroom realities (adaptation/mutual adaptation).
items.rationalization: Effective curricularists practice mutual adaptation: preserving core competencies while modifying pedagogical methods and contexts to match student diversity.

mnemonic.title: Fidelity vs Adaptation
mnemonic.phrase: Faithful to Standards, Flexible in Strategy

items.tosCompetency: Evaluate curriculum implementation fidelity and adaptation
